## New Calls

| Next Deadline | Sponsor | Program | Award Size | Hao Lab Fit (score) | Suggested Team | Link | Added |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pre-proposal 2027-01-07, 2:00 PM ET (full proposal by invitation 2027-03-11) | DoW SERDP (Resource Management and Resilience) | FY 2028 Core Solicitation, SON "Data Fusion for Monitoring Conditions of Natural Infrastructure and Decision Support on Military Installations" | Standard: 2-5 years, cost at proposer's discretion; Limited Scope: up to $350,000, about 1 year | Multi-source remote sensing fusion, ET/soil moisture, decision support (2.2, 2.4); 4 | Yuefeng Hao, Shi Jin, Yifan Gao | [SON page](https://serdp-estcp.mil/workwithus/callforproposal?id=c23979a6-37d8-4cb0-bd28-0c6f144eb3ae) | 2026-11-10 |

### Call Notes

**SERDP FY2028 Core — Data Fusion for Monitoring Conditions of Natural Infrastructure and Decision Support**
- Official pages: [announcement](https://serdp-estcp.mil/newsitems/details/1ad2a7c0-025e-4502-b82e-38b17f5188ed/serdp-releases-fy-2028-core-solicitation),
  [Core solicitation](https://serdp-estcp.mil/workwithus/solicitation?id=0ac3a009-ace9-457c-b92e-bd722e172f90),
  [SON](https://serdp-estcp.mil/workwithus/callforproposal?id=c23979a6-37d8-4cb0-bd28-0c6f144eb3ae),
  and the [FY28 BAA pre-proposal instructions](https://sepub-prod-0001-124733793621-us-gov-west-1.s3.us-gov-west-1.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2026-11/FY28%20SERDP%20CORE%20BAA%20Proposal%20Instructions.pdf?VersionId=gMdAcNjcRrnB_qAuB0cLvKnKMCL85XMY).
- Released 2026-11-05. Universities apply through the BAA. A 5-page
  pre-proposal is required, submitted via SEMS by 2:00 PM ET on 2027-01-07;
  invited full proposals are due 2027-03-11; anticipated awards June 2028.
  Each pre-proposal answers one SON. A webinar is scheduled for 2026-11-20 at
  1:00 PM ET.
- SON objective: develop, validate, and implement statistical data fusion
  for monitoring natural infrastructure on DoW lands and waters. Challenges:
  integrate emerging with legacy monitoring; combine multiple emerging
  technologies; reconcile spatial and temporal scales; fuse spatiotemporal
  data; characterize and propagate uncertainty. Proposals should use public
  earth-observation data, compare fusion against single-source approaches
  (accuracy, coverage, uncertainty, cost, labor), and work closely with
  installation natural-resource or range managers.
- Standard proposals run 2-5 years, cost at the proposer's discretion; Limited
  Scope proposals are up to $350,000 for about one year.
- Fit: the PI's multi-source remote sensing work (Bayesian Model Averaging of
  ET products, FFAR multi-source flash drought framework) and the students'
  computer vision, LiDAR/infrared fusion, and ML skills match the fusion and
  uncertainty challenges. No DoW installation partner is listed in the
  talent pool.

#### Ideas: SERDP FY2028 Core — Data Fusion for Natural Infrastructure Monitoring

**What the SON rewards.** The SON asks for general, rigorous, validated statistical data fusion for natural infrastructure on DoW lands, across five challenges: (1) integrate emerging with legacy monitoring, "including use of contemporary observations to improve inferences from legacy monitoring records"; (2) combine multiple emerging technologies; (3) reconcile spatial and temporal scales; (4) spatiotemporal fusion; (5) characterize and propagate error and uncertainty ([SON](https://serdp-estcp.mil/workwithus/callforproposal?id=c23979a6-37d8-4cb0-bd28-0c6f144eb3ae)). Every proposal must "evaluate the performance, efficiency, and limitations of data-fusion approaches relative to single-source approaches, including differences in accuracy, precision, spatial coverage, uncertainty, cost, and labor requirements", and investigators are expected to "work closely with natural resource or installation range management communities in project design and execution." The named variables lean toward ecology (habitat, species occurrence and abundance), but "environmental variables", "hazard assessments" and "mission relevant environmental conditions" are also in scope, so a drought-stress or fuel-condition product must be framed as a condition variable managers use. Under the FY28 BAA, Relevance is pass/fail and "Technical Merit is significantly more important than Personnel, which is more important than Cost"; technical merit rewards hypothesis-driven tasks with milestones and go/no-go points; an optional "Existing Support" appendix lists overlapping funded work; each pre-proposal answers one SON ([FY28 BAA instructions](https://sepub-prod-0001-124733793621-us-gov-west-1.s3.us-gov-west-1.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2026-11/FY28%20SERDP%20CORE%20BAA%20Proposal%20Instructions.pdf?VersionId=gMdAcNjcRrnB_qAuB0cLvKnKMCL85XMY)). Pre-proposal (5 pages) due **2027-01-07, 2:00 PM ET** in SEMS. **Standard** proposals run 2-5 years; **Limited Scope** proposals are up to **$350,000 for about 1 year**, and the SON invites them for "computationally efficient algorithms, and efficient approaches for working with natural infrastructure datasets of large size and high dimensionality." **Bottom line:** send one pre-proposal to this SON — S1 (Standard, with S2 as its decision aim) if an installation partner and a domain co-investigator are confirmed by about 2026-12-15, otherwise S4 (Limited Scope). The largest weakness: the talent pool shows no DoW installation contact, ecologist, or fire scientist.

##### S1. Uncertainty-aware fusion of legacy and emerging water-stress observations for continuous ecosystem-condition monitoring on Southeastern installations — Pursue (lead, Standard)

**Team.** Yuefeng Hao (PI: ET modeling, Bayesian Model Averaging (BMA), drought, remote sensing, engineering statistics); Yifan Gao (geospatial analysis; scenario and robust-optimization decision layer); Shi Jin (data pipelines and ETL, ML, computer-vision cloud and quality screening). Possible advisors, involvement unconfirmed: ORNL collaborators listed in [hao-lab.md](../talent-pool/labs/hao-lab.md). To recruit, all unconfirmed: a DoW installation natural resources or range partner, an ecologist or forest scientist, and optionally a spatial statistician.

**Research question and approach.** Can hierarchical Bayesian fusion beat every single source, over 2000-present, on accuracy, 30 m to 1 km coverage, and calibrated uncertainty of installation drought-stress and vegetation-condition metrics, and can contemporary high-resolution observations retroactively sharpen the legacy record (SON challenge 1)? Inputs: legacy MODIS-era ET, LST and vegetation indices; VIIRS, ECOSTRESS, HLS, and SMAP; flux towers; installation field records. Tasks: T1 source error characterization (triple and extended collocation; flux-tower validation); T2 hierarchical Bayesian/BMA spatiotemporal fusion with explicit sensor-transition terms (MODIS→VIIRS, ECOSTRESS gaps, HLS cadence); T3 back-casting the legacy record; T4 the required fusion-vs-single-source benchmark (accuracy, precision, coverage, uncertainty, compute cost, field-labor equivalents); T5 a manager-facing condition and uncertainty product co-designed with installation staff. Go/no-go after T1–T2: does fusion beat the best single source on held-out towers or field data?

**Closest existing projects and papers, and the gap.** BMA-ET fuses 30 ET datasets globally against FLUXNET2015 ([ESSD 17, 6445, 2025](https://essd.copernicus.org/articles/17/6445/2025/)); multi-product ET fusion has been tested against 462 flux towers ([Xu et al., AFM 2025](https://lee-lab.yale.edu/sites/default/files/2025-05/xu_afm_2025.pdf)); triple-collocation ET fusion is published ([Atmosphere 15, 1410](https://mdpi.com/2073-4433/15/12/1410)). PML-V2.2 handles MODIS/VIIRS/AVHRR continuity only at 500 m or coarser ([ESSD preprint](https://essd.copernicus.org/preprints/essd-2026-94/essd-2026-94-manuscript-version2.pdf)). ECOSTRESS STARS fuses VIIRS with HLS at 30 m but LP DAAC flags lower-quality periods and VIIRS-dominated artifacts when HLS is sparse ([NASA Earthdata](https://www.earthdata.nasa.gov/data/catalog/lpcloud-eco-l3g-jet-002)). Within SERDP, the nearest precedent is a one-year Interior Alaska multi-sensor project with data through 2017 (page now "Page Not Found"; search snippet only; [project 358c7356](https://serdp-estcp.mil/projects/details/358c7356-da06-46b9-b58d-653849375eb4)); RC25-0189 (LANL, vegetation stress uncertainty) overlaps in wording but its scope could not be verified (snippet only). **Gap:** no funded SERDP project was found that, for Southeastern installations, (a) fuses legacy and emerging ET, soil-moisture, and vegetation records with flux towers, (b) uses explicit error models rather than plain averaging, (c) propagates uncertainty to a decision metric, and (d) reports cost and labor against single-source products.

**Novelty.** Real but methodologically incremental: sensor-transition and back-casting terms, uncertainty carried to a manager-facing metric, and the cost/labor benchmark. Do not pitch it as "BMA of ET extended".

**Why us.** PI's multi-source ET fusion record: generalized complementary relationship models with BMA over China (*AFM* 279, 2019); BMA of hydrological drivers of ET over Northeast Asia (*J. Hydrol.* 607, 2022); co-author, "Integration of multiple drought indices using a triple collocation approach" (*SERRA* 36, 2022); co-author, Simple Taylor Skill Fusion merged ET (ISRS 2018); soil-water-index Priestley-Taylor ET (*AFM* 279, 2019); ET partitioning across biomes (*J. Hydrol.* 603, 2021). U.S. observations: flash-drought WUE and recovery (*AFM* 378, 2026), Missouri Ozark AmeriFlux talk (AGU 2024), CONUS heatwave hydrology (*J. Hydrol.* 637, 2024). Co-PI on the FFAR grant "A multi-source remote sensing-based framework and decision-support tool for flash droughts and floods under climate change" ($434,038, from 04/2024). Lead author of CIVE v1.0 (*Ecological Indicators*, under second revision). Teaches IE 200 Engineering Statistics and IE 465/565 Applied Data Science. Shi Jin built a 350K-paper ETL and retrieval platform with ingestion-time schema validation. Note: the PI's BMA papers cover East Asia, not U.S. installations.

**Fundability.** Hits SON challenges 1, 3, 4, and 5; uses public earth-observation data; builds the mandatory benchmark in as T4; the hypothesis-driven tasks and go/no-go match the BAA's technical-merit language. Weak on installation engagement and Personnel until an installation partner and an ecologist co-investigator are confirmed. Fits a 3-year Standard proposal; typical award size not stated.

**Risks.** (1) No DoW installation partner or access to installation field records — the biggest risk to Relevance and Personnel. (2) Reviewers may see drought/ET as peripheral to species and habitat; tie metrics to at-risk species habitat condition, training-land condition, and burn windows. (3) Overlap with the FFAR grant and October idea G1 (see below) must be declared in Existing Support. (4) Flux-tower density near candidate installations not checked.

**Verdict: Pursue.** Frame on legacy-to-emerging continuity and uncertainty; name 2-3 Southeastern installations only once a partner confirms; add an ecologist or fire/forest co-investigator; prepare a one-page AmeriFlux pilot (fused vs. single-source) as supporting data.

##### S2. Flash drought to fuel-condition fusion for prescribed-burn windows and wildfire risk on Southeastern training lands — Revise (Aim 3 of S1)

**Team.** Hao (flash drought, soil moisture), Gao (burn-window decision layer), Jin (ML). Possible collaborators, unconfirmed: Jiafu Mao, Xiaoying Shi, Mingzhou Jin (co-authors on the wildfire review). Missing: a fire or fuels scientist and an installation fire-management partner.

**Approach.** Fuse SMAP and in-situ soil moisture, ET/LST flash-drought indicators, Sentinel-1 SAR and HLS vegetation water signals, and public fuel-moisture data from SERDP-facilitated burn campaigns ([Fort Stewart 2022](https://wifire-data.sdsc.edu/dataset/2022_fortstewart2022prescribedburncampaignfuelmoisturedata); [Eglin 2023](https://wifire-data.sdsc.edu/dataset/2023_fuelmoisturecontentdatafromthe2023departmentofdefensewildlandfirescienceinitiativeegli)) into calibrated live fuel moisture content (LFMC) and drought-stress maps with uncertainty; test whether they improve burn-window and fire-risk decisions over single-source indices.

**Closest work and gap.** LFMC remote sensing is mostly western U.S.: Sentinel-1 + Landsat-8 physics-assisted RNN ([Konings Lab](https://koningslab.stanford.edu/research/wildfire-behavior)); MODIS-only CONUS deep-learning projections ([Miller et al. 2023, IJWF](https://www.publish.csiro.au/wf/Fulltext/WF22188)); a 2025 foundation-model preprint ([arXiv 2506.20132](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2506.20132v2)). SERDP NH24-9046 collects burn-day fuel and weather data but builds no satellite fusion product ([NH24-9046](https://serdp-estcp.mil/projects/details/ace90b68-342a-4c56-8aec-f5dd4cf061db)). 2026 Southern Area advisories reported D3-D4 drought and reduced live fuel moisture driving fire behavior ([SACC 2026-05-14](https://gacc.nifc.gov/sacc/resources/predictive/Fuels_and_Fire_Behavior_Advisory_Southeastern_Coastal_Plain_051426.pdf)). No study fusing Southeast flash drought with LFMC was found (a search result, not proof).

**Why us.** Flash-drought papers (*AFM* 378, 2026; *J. Hydrol.* 624, 2023); soil moisture review (*npj CAS* 8, 2025); co-author, "Wildfire–Power Grid Interactions" (*RSER* 232, 2026) and the submitted review "Living with Fire in the Humid Southeastern US" (*Earth-Science Reviews*, under review). No fire-behavior or field-fuels record in the talent pool.

**Verdict: Revise.** Make it S1's decision-application aim. Split out only with a fire-science co-PI and an installation fire-program contact, and never send both to this SON.

##### S3. UAS + LiDAR + satellite computer-vision fusion for habitat and vegetation structure — Drop

Already well funded in SERDP: RC24-8162 terrestrial laser scanning in pine ecosystems ([RC24-8162](https://serdp-estcp.mil/projects/details/01612720-0b87-4cb5-8503-eb904fc67862)); RC-201667 multi-sensor airborne mapping ([RC-201667](https://serdp-estcp.mil:443/projects/details/8afe3241-365b-4fd7-a93c-bb141491ce8b)); RC19-5218 and RC18-5187 UAS at Marine Corps installations ([RC19-5218](https://serdp-estcp.mil/projects/details/9dd0dd09-5acd-4e88-a1c7-52451272a96d); [RC18-5187](https://serdp-estcp.mil/projects/details/49ff1f14-56a2-4fe9-bf10-84c46f34386b)); the literature is crowded too ([Remote Sensing 18, 1796](https://mdpi-res.com/d_attachment/remotesensing/remotesensing-18-01796/article_deploy/remotesensing-18-01796.pdf)). Shi Jin's infrared + LiDAR and YOLO/EfficientNet work is industrial (substation digital twin), and the talent pool lists no ecology, forestry, or LiDAR publications. Salvage only as a covariate and quality-screening task inside S1.

##### S4. Scalable spatiotemporal fusion with calibrated uncertainty for large natural-infrastructure datasets (Limited Scope, up to $350K, about 1 year) — Revise (fallback to S1)

**Team.** Hao (PI; statistics and fusion), Jin (ML, pipelines), Gao (ML-assisted optimization, a stated interest).

**Approach.** An ML emulator of the S1 hierarchical Bayesian fusion that reproduces the posterior at a fraction of the compute, with conformal or ensemble calibration checked against triple-collocation error estimates, tested on 30 m multi-decade stacks for one or two installations against single-source products.

**Gap and fit.** No calibrated-uncertainty ML emulator of multi-sensor ET or condition fusion for installations was found (search not exhaustive). Matches the SON's explicit Limited Scope invitation and the "minimal supporting data" situation of a new Assistant Professor.

**Risks.** A pure-methods framing can fail the pass/fail Relevance screen unless tied to one installation variable and one user.

**Verdict: Revise.** Do not submit with S1. Decision rule: by about 2026-12-15, if an installation partner and an ecology or fire co-investigator are confirmed, submit S1 (with S2 as an aim); otherwise submit S4, tied to one variable (drought stress or fuel condition) and public data, as proof of concept for an FY2029 S1.

## Ideas Overview

Ideas for the SERDP SON were screened with the deep-research skill against the SON and BAA text, SERDP-ESTCP project pages, and the literature; research notes are in [ideas/2026-11-10/](ideas/2026-11-10/), and "why us" claims use only facts in [talent-pool/labs/hao-lab.md](../talent-pool/labs/hao-lab.md) and [talent-pool/resources/hao-lab/](../talent-pool/resources/hao-lab/).

### Summary of verdicts

| Call | Idea | Verdict | One-line why us |
|---|---|---|---|
| SERDP FY2028 Core (Data Fusion SON) | S1. Uncertainty-aware legacy-to-emerging water-stress fusion for ecosystem condition on Southeastern installations | Pursue (lead, Standard) | PI's BMA ET fusion, triple-collocation drought-index, and Taylor-skill ET merging papers, plus flash-drought flux-tower work and the FFAR multi-source framework (Co-PI) |
| SERDP FY2028 Core | S2. Flash drought to fuel-condition fusion for burn windows and wildfire risk | Revise (Aim 3 of S1) | Flash-drought papers and co-authorship of the RSER 2026 wildfire-grid review and the submitted humid-Southeast fire review |
| SERDP FY2028 Core | S3. UAS + LiDAR + satellite CV fusion for habitat structure | Drop | Space occupied by RC24-8162, RC-201667, RC19-5218, RC18-5187; Jin's LiDAR fusion is industrial |
| SERDP FY2028 Core | S4. Calibrated-uncertainty ML emulator of the fusion engine (Limited Scope) | Revise (fallback to S1) | PI's fusion record plus Jin's 350K-scale ETL; fits the SON's Limited Scope invitation |

### Which call should host which idea

- **One pre-proposal goes to this SON:** S1 (Standard, with S2 as Aim 3) or S4 (Limited Scope), by the 2026-12-15 decision rule. They share one fusion engine and would read as duplicates. S3 survives only as a task inside S1.
- **Overlap with ideas carried in [summaries/2026-10.md](summaries/2026-10.md):** the closest is NSF GEO Core **G1** (flash-drought recovery process science in humid Southeastern ecosystems, no decision support). S1/S2 are a monitoring product plus installation decisions; they may share data pipelines but not aims or hypotheses. If G1 is submitted, list it in SERDP Existing Support and NSF Current and Pending Support. DOE BER **B1** uses merged ET only as a constraint inside E3SM-RRM and does not conflict. USDA A1712 **R1** and CAREER **K3** are agricultural — keep agricultural land out of S1.
- **Overlap with the FFAR grant (Co-PI, funded):** list it in Existing Support with one sentence on how S1 differs (DoW natural lands; explicit error models propagated to an installation decision metric; legacy-to-emerging continuity; the cost/labor benchmark). The talent pool gives only the FFAR title, so confirm its scope and data-reuse terms with the FFAR lead PI first.

### Open items and limits

- **Team facts:** every "why us" item was matched to the PI CV or [hao-lab.md](../talent-pool/labs/hao-lab.md). The talent pool documents no DoW installation contact, ecologist, fire scientist, letter of support, or ORNL funding arrangement; every collaborator named is a candidate only. Gao's ML-for-optimization work is a stated interest, not a publication.
- **Verification limits:** several SERDP-ESTCP project pages return "Page Not Found" after a site reorganization (Interior Alaska project; RC25-0189 and RC25-4949 news item) and are known from snippets only. FY2025-2026 resource-area new-start lists could not be retrieved, and the directory could not be keyword-searched. NSF, NASA, and USGS award databases were not queried for installation-scale ET fusion. Typical award size is not stated.
- **Actions before 2027-01-07:** attend the 2026-11-20 webinar and ask whether drought, ET, and fuel-condition variables are in scope alongside species and habitat; by about 2026-12-15 secure a Southeastern installation partner and an ecology or fire co-investigator; hand-search the SERDP-ESTCP directory for fusion, ET, drought, and fuel moisture; build the AmeriFlux pilot page; prepare the Existing Support appendix (FFAR, plus G1 if pending).

### Considered but not listed

- SERDP FY2028 Core, other SONs: "Evaluating Performance of Resource

G27AS00170 and the TNWRRC funding page were opened with curl. TNWRRC's
FY2027 internal pre-proposal call and deadline were not found on its site.

## New Calls

| Next Deadline | Sponsor | Program | Award Size | Hao Lab Fit (score) | Suggested Team | Link | Added |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| TNWRRC internal pre-proposal deadline: not stated (call issued in the fall); institute submission to USGS 2026-12-30, 5:00 PM ET | USGS (via Tennessee Water Resources Research Center) | Water Resources Research Act Program Annual Base Grants FY2027 (104(b)) | $202,850 federal per institute for all its projects; 1:1 non-federal match; project 2027-03-01 to 2028-02-29 | Drought/wet cycles, water availability, data center water (2.1, 2.2); 4 | Yuefeng Hao, Yifan Gao, Shi Jin | [Grants.gov](https://simpler.grants.gov/opportunity/0c548397-9fef-4631-ae40-2455ff0904a1) | 2026-11-19 |

### Call Notes

**USGS WRRA 104(b) Annual Base Grants FY2027 (G27AS00170)**
- Official NOFO: [Foa_Content_of_G27AS00170.pdf](https://files.simpler.grants.gov/opportunities/0c548397-9fef-4631-ae40-2455ff0904a1/attachments/88e0e447-501e-4263-ba13-3a27c00b27df/Foa_Content_of_G27AS00170.pdf),
  posted 2026-11-17. Only State Water Resources Research Institutes apply to
  USGS (by 2026-12-30, 5:00 PM ET); each institute receives $202,850 in
  federal funds for its whole program, with a 1:1 non-federal match.
  Anticipated start 2027-03-01, end 2028-02-29.
- USGS emphasis: water-quality and -quantity information, water
  availability, the influence of drought/wet cycles on water resources, and
  emerging water needs; specific emphasis areas are set by each institute
  director.
- Tennessee route: TNWRRC
  ([funding page](https://tnwrrc.tennessee.edu/research/funding.html)) runs
  an internal competition each fall for faculty research proposals and
  graduate student supplemental research grants; faculty at any accredited
  Tennessee college or university may apply. The FY2027 internal deadline
  was not posted; contact TNWRRC now, as it falls before the federal date.
- Note: the PI already holds a 104(b) grant from the previous cycle ("Decision
  Support for TDEC to Reduce Freshwater Withdrawals and Thermal Discharges
  from Data Centers and SMRs in Tennessee"); a new proposal must not
  duplicate it.

#### Ideas: USGS WRRA 104(b) FY2027 via TNWRRC

**Call facts that shape the ideas.** Only state institutes apply to USGS, by **2026-12-30**. Faculty compete earlier in TNWRRC's internal fall pre-proposal round, whose FY2027 date is not posted; in 2019 it closed on **October 18**, about ten weeks before the federal date ([TNWRRC e-News Fall 2019](https://tnwrrc.tennessee.edu/news/enews/Fall2019/enewsFall2019.html); [TNWRRC funding page](https://tnwrrc.tennessee.edu/research/funding.html)), so the window may already be closed — the biggest risk. Each institute gets **$202,850 federal** for its whole program, with a 1:1 match and a 2027-03-01 to 2028-02-29 period ([NOFO](https://simpler.grants.gov/opportunity/0c548397-9fef-4631-ae40-2455ff0904a1)); Tennessee's past allocation ran about $97K–$165K ([TNWRRC Flash Talk 2022](https://isse.utk.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/5/2022/09/2-TNWRRC-Flash-Talk_2022.pdf)). A realistic faculty ask is about $30K–$60K federal (an estimate, not a TNWRRC figure; Kentucky caps FY2026 projects at $25K, [KWRI](https://kwri.uky.edu/copy-of-usgs-grant-applications)). TNWRRC also runs graduate student supplemental grants (about $5K in the past). Each project needs a "who wants it and why" statement; at least 25% of the institute's package must support EO14239 (local preparedness) and SO3444 (strategic AI); USGS screens every project for "overlap or duplication". The PI already holds a 104(b) TDEC award on data center and SMR withdrawals (from 01/2027), so the new proposal must stay off data centers. **Bottom line:** submit **I1** as the faculty pre-proposal (with I2 as its test case) and pair it with the student grant **I4** (Yifan Gao).

##### I1. Flash-drought triggers for Tennessee public water supply, tested on the fall 2026 drought — Pursue (lead faculty proposal)

**Team.** Yuefeng Hao (PI: flash drought, ET, drought indices); Yifan Gao (geospatial; leads I4); Shi Jin from Spring 2027 (ML benchmark). To recruit, all unconfirmed: a Duck River-area utility, the Duck River Agency, or a TDEC contact for a letter.

**Research question and approach.** Which sub-monthly indicators — soil moisture (satellite and model), ET and evaporative stress (Priestley–Taylor and BMA ET), or a triple-collocation combination — give the earliest skillful warning of the low flows and groundwater declines that matter at water-supply intakes, and how can they become trigger levels a community water system can adopt? (1) Retrospective analysis of past Southeast fall droughts (e.g., 2007, 2016, 2019, 2023) in the Duck River and one comparison HUC-8; (2) skill and lead-time scoring against USGS streamflow and groundwater percentiles; (3) the fall 2026 drought and its 2027 recovery as an out-of-sample test; (4) a trigger table and an open dataset for TDEC, utilities, and the Duck River planning process. Interpretable ML serves only as a benchmark (the SO3444 element).

**Closest work and the gap.** The fall 2026 event went from late-September dryness to Extreme Drought in Middle Tennessee within weeks ([WSMV](https://www.wsmv.com/2026/10/30/drought-worsens-across-middle-tennessee/); [NWS Huntsville 2026-10-20](https://www.weather.gov/media/hun/DGT/DGT_HUN_10202026.pdf)). Tennessee's 2010 drought plan "does not specify monitoring indicators nor the threshold values that would trigger drought declaration", while local systems keep their own triggers ([NewsChannel9/AP](https://newschannel9.com/news/local/noaa-report-tennessee-drought-plan-lacks-triggers-water-oversight-infrastructure-national-oceanic-atmospheric-administration-water-quality-public-health-ecosystems)). A draft 2026 Duck River Regional Drought Management Plan is listed but its PDF could not be opened ([draft URL](https://www.tn.gov/content/dam/tn/environment/water/water-public-notices/ppo_water_2026-09-04-draft-2026-duck-river-regional-drought-management-plan.pdf)). Sub-monthly (8–21 day) indicators give earlier warning for Southeast water supply ([Drought.gov 2025](https://www.drought.gov/news/facing-future-droughts-lessons-southeasts-2023-fall-flash-drought-2025-12-02)); soil-moisture indicators alone caught a 2022 Connecticut flash drought before declarations ([EGU26-8499](https://meetingorganizer.copernicus.org/EGU26/EGU26-8499.html)). Closest funded work is national AI flash-drought forecasting ([NSF 2616279](https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/showAward?AWD_ID=2616279)); NSF searches for "flash drought" + "water supply" returned no awards ([NSF API](https://api.nsf.gov/services/v1/awards.json?keyword=%22flash%20drought%22%20%22water%20supply%22)); the PI's FFAR tool targets agriculture. **Gap:** no study was found that calibrates flash-drought indicators to Tennessee public-water-supply triggers or tests them on a live event.

**Novelty.** Applied and regional, not a new forecasting method: turning sub-monthly indicators into intake-relevant triggers validated out of sample on 2026 — the kind of applied work 104(b) funds.

**Why us.** Flash-drought WUE and recovery (*AFM* 378, 2026) and the Missouri Ozark AmeriFlux recovery talk (AGU 2024); drought-index comparison for recovery time (*SERRA* 36, 2022, lead author); co-author, "Integration of multiple drought indices using a triple collocation approach" (*SERRA* 36, 2022); heatwave hydrology (*J. Hydrol.* 637, 2024); co-author on terrestrial water storage (*J. Hydrol.* 635, 2024); soil-water-index Priestley–Taylor ET and complementary-relationship BMA ET (*AFM* 279, 2019); Co-PI on the FFAR flash-drought decision-support grant ($434,038, from 04/2024); ongoing Xi–Hao–Leib–M. Jin irrigation decision-support paper under flash drought and flood risk.

**Fundability.** WRRI priorities Water Hazards or Water Scarcity and Availability; focus categories DROUGHT, WATER SUPPLY, HYDROLOGY; matches the NOFO's drought/wet-cycle emphasis and EO14239; a Middle Tennessee "who wants it" story is on public record; feasible in one year on public data with one graduate student.

**Risks.** Internal deadline may have passed; no utility or agency partner documented; trigger skill ideally needs intake or pumpage records (start with USGS gauges and wells; TDEC registration data are not public, [TDEC page](https://www.tn.gov/environment/program-areas/wr-water-resources/water-quality/water-withdrawal-registration-program.html), snippet only); 2026 recovery may be partial by 2028-02; lead with Middle Tennessee (West Tennessee status unverified).

**Verdict: Pursue.**

##### I2. Fall 2026 flash drought event and streamflow, groundwater, and soil-moisture recovery study — Revise (merge as I1's test-case aim)

Standalone it is a one-event case study; Southeast flash-drought event studies already exist ([Georgia headwater catchment, USGS](https://www.usgs.gov/publications/ecohydrological-response-a-forested-headwater-catchment-a-flash-drought-southeastern); [2019 attribution, NOAA](https://repository.library.noaa.gov/view/noaa/54601), snippet only; [2023 synthesis](https://www.drought.gov/news/facing-future-droughts-lessons-southeasts-2023-fall-flash-drought-2025-12-02)). Why us: recovery papers (*SERRA* 36, 2022; *J. Hydrol.* 622, 2023; *AFM* 378, 2026). It overlaps NSF GEO **G1** (ecosystem recovery), so keep it on water resources. Make it I1's out-of-sample test and recovery aim.

##### I3. Drought-conditioned sub-basin water availability for Tennessee's projected large-load (data center) growth — Revise (backup; not this cycle)

Fits "water availability", and no NSF award on "data center" + "water availability" was found ([NSF API](https://api.nsf.gov/services/v1/awards.json?keyword=%22data%20center%22%20%22water%20availability%22)); the USGS Water Mission Area data center work covers on-site cooling only ([Zintellect DOI-USGS-2026-33](https://www.zintellect.com/Opportunity/Details/DOI-USGS-2026-33)). Why us: funded 104(b) TDEC grant (PI), ISSE footprint grant (PI), submitted paper "Regional screening of electricity-related water consumption for projected data-center load growth" (*Water Resources and Industry*, under review). Those strengths are also the duplication risk: it sits beside the 104(b) TDEC grant, 104g **U1/U2**, CAREER **K1/K2**, and EWRE **E1**. Hold it; if used, reframe to drought-year supply at HUC-10 scale with large loads as one demand scenario, and move it to 104(g) or CAREER.

##### I4. NLP inventory of Tennessee community water system drought triggers (graduate student supplemental grant) — Pursue (linked to I1)

**Team.** Yifan Gao (student lead; full-time PhD student since Fall 2026); Hao (advisor). Shi Jin starts Spring 2027 and should not lead a fall 2026 student application.

**Approach.** Collect publicly posted drought management plans of Tennessee community water systems (required by TDEC), extract trigger indicators, thresholds, source types, and response stages into a source-linked inventory, and compare what utilities use with what I1's indicators signaled in 2026. Plans found online include MLGW's ([2022](https://www.mlgw.com/images/content/files/pdf/MLGW_DroughtManagementPlanFinal9202022.pdf)) and Nashville Metro Water's ([2016](https://filetransfer.nashville.gov/portals/0/sitecontent/WaterServices/docs/reports/Metro%20Water%20Services%2016%20Drought%20Management%20Plan%20-%20%2006-17-2016.pdf)) (search listings only, not opened).

**Gap and why us.** No inventory of Tennessee utility drought triggers was found; USGS harmonizes national withdrawal data, not plan triggers ([USGS](https://pubs.usgs.gov/publication/70273350), snippet). Gao's undergraduate NLP and information-extraction research and source-linked dataset approach, plus the PI's drought-index record. Small, AI-enabled (SO3444), and sized to a student grant.

**Risks.** Coverage depends on how many systems post plans; keep it on water supply, not data centers. The original version (AI audit of TDEC registration records) depends on unconfirmed data access and overlaps 104g **U4** — Revise/Drop that version.

**Verdict: Pursue** as I1's student companion.

##### I5. Student grant on data center siting under water stress — Drop

Duplicates the funded 104(b) TDEC grant and both students' ongoing siting papers, reads as infrastructure planning rather than water resources research, and Shi Jin is not yet enrolled for a fall 2026 call. A water-stress layer belongs in the TDEC project or CAREER **K1**.

## Ideas Overview

Ideas for this call were screened with the deep-research skill against the NOFO, TNWRRC pages, NSF and USAspending records, and the literature; research notes are in [ideas/2026-11-19/](ideas/2026-11-19/), and "why us" claims use only facts in [talent-pool/labs/hao-lab.md](../talent-pool/labs/hao-lab.md) and [talent-pool/resources/hao-lab/](../talent-pool/resources/hao-lab/).

### Summary of verdicts

| Call | Idea | Verdict | One-line why us |
|---|---|---|---|
| USGS 104(b) FY2027 via TNWRRC | I1. Flash-drought triggers for Tennessee public water supply, tested on fall 2026 | Pursue (lead faculty proposal) | Flash-drought recovery, triple-collocation drought-index, and PT/BMA ET papers, plus the FFAR flash-drought grant (Co-PI) applied to a new sector |
| USGS 104(b) FY2027 via TNWRRC | I2. Fall 2026 drought event and recovery study | Revise (I1's test-case aim) | Drought recovery-time and recovery papers (SERRA 2022, J. Hydrol. 2023, AFM 2026) |
| USGS 104(b) FY2027 via TNWRRC | I3. Drought-conditioned sub-basin availability for large-load growth | Revise (backup; move to 104g or CAREER) | Funded 104(b) TDEC and ISSE grants and the submitted electricity-water paper (also the overlap risk) |
| USGS 104(b) FY2027 via TNWRRC | I4. NLP inventory of community water system drought triggers (student grant) | Pursue (linked to I1) | Gao's NLP and information-extraction background plus the PI's drought-index expertise |
| USGS 104(b) FY2027 via TNWRRC | I5. Student grant on data center siting under water stress | Drop | Duplicates the 104(b) TDEC grant and both students' siting papers |

### Which call should host which idea

- **This call: I1 (faculty) plus I4 (student)**, with I2 inside I1. Both are about drought and water supply and do not touch data centers or SMRs.
- **Funded 104(b) TDEC grant:** all data center and SMR withdrawal and thermal-discharge work stays there (hence I3 and I5 are not submitted). Ask TNWRRC whether a PI with a current 104(b) award can apply again.
- **FFAR grant (Co-PI):** I1 reuses its multi-source framework for public water supply instead of agriculture; list FFAR in current support with that one-sentence difference, and confirm its scope and data-reuse terms with the FFAR lead PI.
- **Ideas in [summaries/2026-10.md](summaries/2026-10.md):** keep I1/I2 off ecosystem carbon (GEO **G1**); no conflict with USDA **R1**; do not add allocation optimization to I1 (CAREER **K3**). The closest overlap is NOAA **N2** (heat and flash-drought thresholds for agriculture and rural water, folded into N1): if N1 goes to NOAA, keep its water module on NOAA-heat-driven thresholds and I1 on soil-moisture and ET triggers for Tennessee intakes, and list each in the other's pending support. 104g **U1/U2/U4**, CAREER **K1/K2**, and EWRE **E1** overlap I3, I4's original version, and I5, not I1.
- **Ideas in [2026-11-10.md](2026-11-10.md):** SERDP **S1/S2** (DoW natural lands) may share ET and soil-moisture pipelines with I1 but not aims; list them as pending if submitted.

### Open items and limits

- **Deadline first:** contact the TNWRRC program office this week — is the FY2027 internal window open, what are the per-project and student caps and page limits, and are repeat PIs allowed? If closed, carry I1 and I4 to the FY2028 round.
- **Team facts:** every "why us" item was checked against the PI CV, [hao-lab.md](../talent-pool/labs/hao-lab.md), or the student files. No utility, TDEC, Duck River Agency, or USGS Tennessee Water Science Center partner or letter is documented; all partners are candidates only. A not-funded 2025 BSF proposal on AI flash flood and flash drought early warning in the CV is reusable draft text, not an asset.
- **Verification limits:** the Duck River draft plan, the Duck River Watershed Planning Partnership recommendations, and the TDEC registration page returned stub pages; Tennessee 104(b) projects for FY2020–FY2026 and the national WRRI project database were not reached; West Tennessee drought status and the number of posted utility drought plans were not checked; per-project amounts are estimates.
- **Before submission:** draft the 300-word abstract and "who wants it and why" statement around the Duck River and Middle Tennessee drought; map I1 to EO14239 and SO3444; seek one utility or agency letter; confirm the FFAR scope; plan the 1:1 match with UT sponsored programs.

### Considered but not listed

- Army Contracting Command Broad Agency Announcement for Fundamental AI
  Research (W519TC-25-S-0001): a FY2025 forecast with no dates (not open).
- NSF Science of Learning and Augmented Intelligence; NSF CyberAI SFS:
  education and learning-science programs outside Hao Lab directions
  (score 1-2).

  deployment or education programs, not research on Hao Lab topics
  (score 1-2).

## New Calls

| 2027-01-15, 11:59 PM PST | CLaSH — NSF Center for Land Surface Hazards (NSF-EAR 2425607; awards issued by the University of Michigan) | CLaSH Small Grant Program 2026-27 | $20,000-$40,000 incl. indirect costs; 5-9 awards; up to 12 months from 2027-05-01 | Soil moisture/ET and flash drought as preconditioning of hazard cascades; remote sensing and AI (2.2, 2.4); 4 | Yuefeng Hao, Yifan Gao, Shi Jin (+ recommended collaborators below) | [Program page](https://www.geoclash.org/small-grant-program-2026-2027/) | 2026-11-20 |

### Call Notes

**CLaSH Small Grant Program 2026-27**
- Official sources: [program page](https://www.geoclash.org/small-grant-program-2026-2027/)
  and [RFP PDF](https://www.geoclash.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/CLASH-Small-Grant-RFP-2027.pdf)
  (updated 2026-10-30). Proposals due 2027-01-15, 11:59 PM PST, through the
  application portal; notifications early to mid April 2027; project
  2027-05-01 to 2028-04-30.
- 5-9 awards of $20,000-$40,000 including indirect costs. Allowed: salary for
  faculty, postdocs and students, travel, equipment, analysis. Not allowed:
  subawards, participant support, computers.
- Eligibility: PIs at U.S. institutions eligible for NSF funding who can serve
  as an NSF PI; "early-career scientists and investigators are strongly
  encouraged to apply."
- Format: cover page, 250-word abstract, 5-page project description (2
  figures), biosketch, current and pending support, optional letters of
  collaboration, budget in the CLaSH Excel template.
- Priority areas: (1) cross-observatory hypothesis testing at the CLaSH
  Hazard Observatories (Alaska, Appalachia, Puerto Rico, Southern California;
  this year cross-observatory work or Puerto Rico/Alaska is favored);
  (2) modeling the hazard cascade (triggers, hillslope-channel coupling,
  runout, flooding; CSDMS/Landlab/BMI; "ML/AI applications ... are especially
  welcome"); (3) remote sensing and AI at scale (InSAR, FAIR AI-ready
  datasets and benchmarks); (4) event-driven investigations and new hazard
  types.
- Review: intellectual merit, broader impacts, relevance (cascade gaps;
  "link two or more processes or observatories"), innovation and
  collaboration (new partnerships), feasibility.
- Fit: the CLaSH strategic plan names soil moisture as a trigger condition and
  "wet–dry cycles" as preconditioning, and says it wants "climatologists and
  civil engineers"; no observatory lists a drought or ET lead. That is Hao
  Lab's strongest area. The Appalachia observatory (Kentucky) is the nearest
  to Tennessee. Hao Lab has no landslide or geomorphology record, so partners
  are essential.

#### Past winners: CLaSH Small Grant Program

CLaSH has not published a list of funded small grants (website, both
small-grant pages, three 2026 newsletters, and web searches were checked). The
2025-26 round was the first since Center operations began in October 2025.
Two indirect cases were found:
- A University of Washington professor is named a "small grants recipient"
  in the [2026 Annual Meeting recap](https://www.geoclash.org/2026-annual-meeting/);
  the talk integrated NASA products, earth-surface models, and AI ensembles
  for hazard-chain prediction.
- A "CLASH mini-grant" to two University of Kentucky / Kentucky Geological
  Survey researchers supported Hurricane Helene debris-flow runout and
  initiation-threshold work ([case studies](https://www.geoclash.org/case-studies/));
  it is unclear whether this was the Small Grant Program.

Patterns (weak, from two cases plus the [strategic plan](https://www.geoclash.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/CLaSH-1.0-Five-Year-Strategic-Plan.pdf)):
both winners tie directly to an existing CLaSH activity (the Modeling
Collaboratory; event response at the Appalachia observatory); both mix
observations or remote sensing with process modeling and AI; the plan gives
"priority for early-career researchers", wants new expertise, and wants work
"meaningfully distinct" from what the Center already funds. Ideas below copy
these features: tie to an observatory or the Modeling Collaboratory, combine
remote sensing + modeling + AI, bring hydro-climate expertise CLaSH lacks, and
link two processes or two observatories. Ask the CLaSH program contact for
the 2025-26 funded-project list before writing.

#### Ideas: CLaSH Small Grant Program 2026-27

Thirteen short ideas from different angles; the two marked Pursue are
evaluated in full below. Submit **one** proposal (CL1), with CL3 as the
alternative.

| # | Idea | Angle | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| CL1 | Does flash drought and ET-driven drying in the weeks to months before a storm raise or lower landslide rainfall thresholds? Helene (2024) and eastern Kentucky (2022) vs. Maria (2017) and Fiona (2022) in Puerto Rico | Drought → rain → landslides; remote sensing; cross-observatory | **Pursue (lead)** |
| CL2 | FAIR, AI-ready antecedent-wetness data cube (soil moisture + ET, triple collocation + BMA, with uncertainty) for the observatories | Data fusion; benchmark dataset | Revise: CL1's deliverable |
| CL3 | How long does a cascade last? Vegetation, ET, and water-use recovery on landslide scars of three ages (Maria 2017, Kentucky 2022, Helene 2024), and whether slow recovery predicts reactivation | Long tail of the cascade; recovery; computer vision | **Pursue (alternative)** |
| CL4 | Landslide, debris-flow, and flood-corridor exposure of power lines, substations, and data-center sites in the southern Appalachians, as a constraint in the lab's siting models | Infrastructure exposure; optimization | Revise: broader-impacts module of CL1 |
| CL5 | Landlab/BMI component replacing static recharge with satellite-constrained, drought-aware ET and recharge in landslide probability | Cascade modeling; CSDMS | Revise: CL1's modeling aim; needs a Landlab partner |
| CL6 | Fire-then-storm debris flows in the humid Southeast (building on the PI's submitted Southeast fire review) | Wildfire → rain → debris flow; new hazard type | Revise: needs a fire-geomorphology partner and site data |
| CL7 | Future frequency of dry-then-wet sequences from E3SM regionally refined output with ORNL collaborators | Trigger climatology; Earth system modeling | Revise: too large for 12 months; small version inside CL1 |
| CL8 | Deep-learning mapping of debris fans and runout from lidar in Kentucky | Computer vision; lidar | Drop: already a planned CLaSH core task |
| CL9 | NLP-built inventory of landslide impacts on roads, power, and water from agency and news text | Impacts; NLP/ETL | Revise: small task inside CL4 or CL1 |
| CL10 | Robust-optimization design of soil-moisture or piezometer sensor networks at an observatory | Monitoring design; systems engineering | Revise: pitch as a collaboration with an observatory team |
| CL11 | Fall 2026 Tennessee flash drought as a natural experiment for the next storms | Event-driven | Drop: overlaps I1/I2 in [2026-11-19.md](2026-11-19.md); no slope data |
| CL12 | Snowmelt and soil-moisture preconditioning of debris flows at the Alaska observatory | Alaska (favored) | Drop: no site expertise or tribal partner |
| CL13 | "AI for hazard cascades" module in IE 465/565 Applied Data Science using CLaSH open data | Education | Drop as standalone: CL1's broader impacts |

##### CL1. Does flash drought set up or suppress the landslide cascade? Wet-dry preconditioning of rainfall-triggered landslides in Appalachia and Puerto Rico — Pursue (lead)

**Team.** Yuefeng Hao (PI; ET, soil moisture, flash drought); Yifan Gao (data pipeline, ML screening of predictors); Shi Jin (from Spring 2027; image and time-series ML). ORNL collaborators as possible unfunded advisors (unconfirmed). Partners: see "Recommended collaborators" (all unconfirmed; no subawards allowed, so they join by letter or as a same-institution co-PI).

**Research question and approach.** Does the hydro-climate state 1-90 days before an extreme storm (flash-drought onset, ET deficit, root-zone soil-moisture anomaly) shift the rainfall needed to trigger landslides, and does the sign differ between temperate Appalachian and tropical Puerto Rican soils? Hypotheses: drought-wetting cycles lower thresholds in clay-rich regolith through cracks and preferential flow (H1); deep root-zone drying adds storage and raises thresholds (H2); the net effect depends on soil and critical-zone class (H3). Steps: (1) compile existing landslide inventories (Helene, eastern Kentucky 2022, Maria); (2) build daily ET and root-zone soil-moisture histories with the PI's Priestley-Taylor soil-water-index and BMA ET methods plus SMAP and reanalysis; (3) fit antecedent-conditioned rainfall-threshold models per observatory and compare across sites; (4) release the antecedent-wetness cube and code as a FAIR dataset, with a BMI-wrappable threshold function for the CLaSH Modeling Collaboratory.

**Closest existing work and the gap.** Maria landslides were linked to soil moisture 11-13% above average ([GSA Today](https://www.geosociety.org/gsatoday/science/G383A/article.htm), search summary) and Helene landsliding to rain in the days before the storm ([GSA Today 2026](https://www.geosociety.org/gsa-today/january-2026/insights-into-widespread-landsliding-in-southern-appalachia-from-hurricane), search summary): single events, wet anomalies, days not months. A 2026 paper adds SMAP soil moisture to highway landslide thresholds but does not test drought preconditioning or compare sites ([NHESS 26, 3163](https://nhess.copernicus.org/articles/26/3163/2026/nhess-26-3163-2026.pdf), search summary). Puerto Rican hillslopes "aren't always wet" ([USGS](https://www.usgs.gov/publications/hillslopes-humid-tropical-climates-arent-always-wet-implications-hydrologic-response), search summary). NSF RAPID 2629285 collects Helene debris-flow field data, not antecedent hydro-climate ([NSF](https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/showAward?AWD_ID=2629285)); NSF keyword searches for drought or evapotranspiration plus landslide found no award on drought preconditioning. Inside CLaSH, soil-moisture threshold work focuses first on Puerto Rico and Southern California. **Gap:** a drought and ET history (weeks to months) tested as a preconditioning variable across temperate and tropical observatories, including Appalachia.

**Why us.** Soil-water-index Priestley-Taylor ET and complementary-relationship BMA ET (*AFM* 279, 2019); triple-collocation drought-index integration and drought recovery time (*SERRA* 36, 2022); flash-drought WUE and recovery (*AFM* 378, 2026); heatwave hydrology (*J. Hydrol.* 637, 2024); lead author of the soil-moisture review (*npj CAS* 8, 2025); Co-PI on the FFAR multi-source flash drought and flood framework; Topic Lead of the RUBISCO Soil Moisture Working Group mini-workshops. This is the hydro-climate expertise CLaSH says it wants and does not yet have at the observatories.

**Fit to review criteria and past-winner patterns.** Links two processes (drought/ET → rainfall triggering) and two observatories; new discipline and new partnerships; existing data only, so feasible in 12 months and $40K; FAIR dataset, graduate training, and a course module as broader impacts; remote sensing + modeling + AI tied to an observatory, like both known winners.

**Risks.** Many landslides lack exact failure dates (aggregate by storm); satellite soil moisture is coarse and shallow (use ET-based root-zone proxies and show uncertainty); few events per site (add a regional Kentucky storm catalog); reviewers may see overlap with CLaSH's own soil-moisture task (talk to the observatory leads first); the PI has no landslide record (partner letters are essential).

**Verdict: Pursue.** Before writing: ask the CLaSH program contact for the funded-project list; contact the Appalachia observatory partner and a Puerto Rico observatory researcher for inventory access and letters; confirm UT's indirect rate.

##### CL3. How long does a landslide cascade last? Satellite ecohydrologic recovery of landslide and debris-flow scars across three event ages — Pursue (alternative lead)

**Team.** Yuefeng Hao (PI; recovery-time methods); Shi Jin (scar segmentation and change detection, multi-sensor registration); Yifan Gao (pipeline, statistics).

**Research question and approach.** After landslides strip vegetation, how long do greenness, ET, and water-use efficiency take to recover, what controls it (climate, soil, scar size, later drought), and does slow recovery predict reactivation (some Maria slopes reportedly failed again in Fiona)? Build Landsat/Sentinel-2/MODIS vegetation and ET time series on scars and paired controls from existing inventories; estimate recovery time with the PI's drought-recovery framework; release a FAIR scar-recovery dataset across observatories.

**Gap.** The strategic plan asks "How long do cascading hazards last?" and names vegetation loss and regrowth, but lists no recovery-tracking task. Inventories map where landslides happened, not how they recover. A literature search on satellite recovery of landslide scars has **not** been done (such studies exist for earthquake landslides), so novelty is unproven.

**Why us.** Recovery of carbon and water fluxes after drought (*J. Hydrol.* 622, 2023); drought recovery time (*SERRA* 36, 2022); flash-drought WUE and recovery (*AFM* 378, 2026); Shi Jin's YOLO/EfficientNet detection and infrared + LiDAR registration experience.

**Risks.** Novelty unproven; small scars are below Landsat/MODIS resolution; Helene scars are young.

**Verdict: Pursue as the alternative.** Do not submit both. Choose CL3 only if the literature check confirms the gap and a Puerto Rico ecology partner joins.

#### Recommended collaborators: CLaSH Small Grant Program 2026-27

All twelve people are new (none is in the registry as a past collaborator), so the more-than-half-new requirement is met. Nobody has been contacted and none has agreed to anything. Subawards are not allowed, so the practical structure is Hao as PI with a UT Knoxville co-PI, plus collaborators and data partners by letter. Whether co-PIs at other institutions are allowed was not checked (the FAQ was not opened). No candidate states their gender publicly, so gender was not scored. Stephen Hughes, Geology, University of Puerto Rico at Mayagüez | Collaborator with letter; Puerto Rico observatory link | Landslides and sediment after tropical cyclones | CLaSH senior personnel ([Team Bios](https://www.geoclash.org/team-bios/)); NSF [2301379](https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/showAward?AWD_ID=2301379), [2224973](https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/showAward?AWD_ID=2224973) (name matched by institution and topic) | High: priority observatory; minority-serving institution |

## Ideas Overview

Research notes for this call are in [ideas/2026-11-20/](ideas/2026-11-20/). "Why us" claims use only facts in [talent-pool/labs/hao-lab.md](../talent-pool/labs/hao-lab.md) and [talent-pool/resources/hao-lab/](../talent-pool/resources/hao-lab/).

### Summary of verdicts

| Call | Idea | Verdict | One-line why us |
|---|---|---|---|
| CLaSH Small Grant 2026-27 | CL1. Wet-dry preconditioning of landslides across Appalachia and Puerto Rico | Pursue (lead) | PI's ET, soil-moisture, flash-drought, and drought-index papers; hydro-climate expertise CLaSH lacks |
| CLaSH Small Grant 2026-27 | CL3. Ecohydrologic recovery of landslide scars | Pursue (alternative) | PI's drought recovery-time papers plus Shi Jin's computer vision |

| CLaSH Small Grant 2026-27 | CL6, CL10 | Revise (need a partner first) | Southeast fire review; optimization |
| CLaSH Small Grant 2026-27 | CL8, CL11, CL12, CL13 | Drop | — |

### Which call should host which idea

- **CLaSH hosts one proposal: CL1** (with CL2 as its dataset, CL5 as a light modeling hook, CL4 and CL13 as broader impacts). CL3 is the fallback or next year's proposal.
- **Overlap with tracked ideas:** CL1 and CL3 reuse the flash-drought and recovery methods of NSF GEO **G1** ([summaries/2026-10.md](summaries/2026-10.md)) and USGS 104(b) **I1** ([2026-11-19.md](2026-11-19.md)) but predict a different outcome (landslide triggering and scar recovery, not ecosystem fluxes or water-supply triggers). CL2's data fusion resembles SERDP **S1** ([2026-11-10.md](2026-11-10.md)); keep it a small dataset inside CL1. CL4 touches the data center themes of CAREER **K1** and NOAA **N1**; keep it as broader impacts only. List all pending proposals in Current and Pending Support.

### Open items and limits

- Past awardees are not published; patterns rest on two indirect cases. Ask the CLaSH program contact for the 2025-26 funded-project list.
- The FAQ was not opened: whether co-PIs at other institutions or paired proposals are allowed is unknown.
- Several literature items were seen only as search summaries; the scar-recovery literature search (CL3) and the Landlab landslide component check (CL5) were not done.
- Two UT Knoxville faculty profiles and one USGS profile could not be opened (bot check or error); those entries are partly verified.
- No partner has been contacted; none has agreed to anything. UT's indirect rate is not in the talent pool.

### Considered but not listed

- None; this scan covers only the CLaSH call. The regular scan on 2026-11-22 resumes the full search with the wider source list.

###### U1. Tennessee data center water use: hybrid physics-ML estimation validated against independent records — Pursue (merged lead)

**Team:** Yuefeng Hao (PI), Yifan Gao, Shi Jin; Mingzhou Jin as a possible collaborator (UT ISE/ISSE, listed in hao-lab.md; participation not confirmed).

**Research question and approach.** Can Scope 1 water use (direct use from public supply and self-supply) of Tennessee data centers be estimated at the facility or county level with calibrated uncertainty, from public and utility data? Can Scope 2 (thermoelectric water tied to their electricity) be attributed on top of that? The model chain is a hybrid physics-ML estimator: IT load → cooling technology → water-use effectiveness, plus grid mix → plant-level water intensity. It produces probabilistic outputs and is validated on 3–5 Tennessee facilities with utility or permit data obtained through letters of support.

**Closest existing work and gap.** Siddik, Shehabi and Marston (2021) gave the first spatially detailed US water footprint of data centers ([LBNL](https://eta-publications.lbl.gov/bibcite/reference/34978)). The Ren group works at national and peak-capacity scale ([arXiv 2304.03271](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.03271v4); [arXiv 2603.02705](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.02705)). Minnesota Sea Grant funds a facility-level real-time estimation dashboard for Minnesota ([MN Sea Grant](https://seagrant.umn.edu/research/ai-water-impact)). The USGS project above covers Scope 1 only. None found does ML-based, uncertainty-quantified, validated Scope 1+2 estimation for one balancing authority (TVA).

**Novelty.** Methods are incremental, but geography and validation are strong. The project also directly fills the Scope 2 gap that USGS's own project leaves open.

**Why us.** The PI holds the ISSE grant on the local water footprint of AI data centers in Tennessee and the USGS 104b TDEC grant on data center and SMR withdrawals. The PI also has a submitted paper, "Regional screening of electricity-related water consumption for projected data-center load growth" (with Kaylee Jin, *Water Resources and Industry*, under review), which is the direct precursor for Scope 2. Gao's and Jin's ongoing Tennessee Valley siting papers supply the demand side.

**Fundability.** It hits "estimating, validating, forecasting", the AI/ML requirement and "validating results against independent or ground truth data" almost verbatim. Training points (10) are covered by naming Gao and Jin as federally supported students.

**Risks.** Ground-truth access (utility billing at MLGW, KUB and others) is unconfirmed. Whether Tennessee withdrawal registration data are accessible was not verified. $120K over 3 years is a small budget. The program screens for overlap with the 104b project, so the proposal must say plainly that 104b produces a TDEC decision tool while 104g produces validated estimation methods.

**Verdict: Pursue.** Lead with Scope 1 from public supply, as the NOFO frames it, and present Scope 2 as the "associated" component that complements the USGS project.

###### U2. Seasonal, heatwave and flash-drought forecasts of data center water demand under siting-policy scenarios — Pursue (Aim 3 of U1)

**Team:** Yuefeng Hao, Yifan Gao, Shi Jin.

**Research question and approach.** How do weather-driven peak cooling demand and flash-drought or heatwave stress on source water combine with policy-aware build-out (tariffs, moratoria, interconnection queues) to shape future demand on Tennessee public supply?

**Closest existing work and gap.** "Small Bottle, Big Pipe" projects national peak-day capacity needs of 697–1,451 MGD through 2030 ([arXiv 2603.02705](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.02705)). An ACS study finds about 25% of 9,347 data centers face water stress at least one month a year ([ACS](https://www.acs.org/pressroom/presspacs/2026/october/many-data-centers-are-located-where-water-resources-are-limited.html)). None couples policy-aware siting scenarios with process-based flash-drought and heatwave hydrology at local supply scale.

**Novelty.** Real. It joins three things no one has joined.

**Why us.** The PI's papers on heatwave effects on CONUS hydrology (*J. Hydrol.* 2024) and on flash-drought ecosystem effects and recovery. Shi Jin's "Siting Under Moving Rules" (tariff- and moratorium-aware siting in the Tennessee Valley) and Yifan Gao's robust siting under interconnection-queue uncertainty.

**Fundability.** It answers "forecast future scenarios" and "seasonal variability", and supports EO14239 local preparedness.

**Risks.** Forecasts cannot be validated within the award, and on its own the idea reads as planning. That is why it is an aim of U1, not a standalone proposal.

**Verdict: Pursue as Aim 3 of U1.**

###### U3. Computer-vision detection of data center cooling technology — Revise (Aim 1 data layer)

**Team:** Shi Jin, Yuefeng Hao.

**Approach and change.** The original idea, quantifying evaporative loss from Landsat, ECOSTRESS or MODIS thermal and ET signals, is physically weak. Cooling towers are building-scale. ECOSTRESS is 70 m, ET algorithms are calibrated for vegetation, and its industrial use so far is detecting once-through thermal plumes ([ECOSTRESS poster](https://ecostress.jpl.nasa.gov/downloads/other/ECOSTRESS_aquatic_applications_poster.pdf)). The revised version classifies cooling technology (wet towers, dry or adiabatic coolers, chillers) from high-resolution imagery, following WRI's satellite method for power plants. That method reached 90% precision on cooling type and 69% on water demand across 200 US plants ([WRI](https://www.wri.org/research/methodology-estimate-water-demand-thermal-power-plants-data-scarce-regions-using-satellite)). Thermal anomalies serve only as signals of operating status.

**Gap.** No satellite or aerial detection of data center cooling type was found.

**Why us.** Shi Jin's YOLO/EfficientNet inspection models and SLAM-based infrared + LiDAR registration for a substation digital twin; the PI's MODIS and multi-source remote sensing work. Shi Jin starts in Spring 2027, so this aim should be scheduled from year 1, semester 2.

**Verdict: Revise.** Use it as the "observing" input to U1, not as a standalone proposal.

###### B1. Water availability for Tennessee Valley energy expansion under compound flash drought-heat extremes: AI-enhanced E3SM-RRM coupled to large-load siting — Pursue

**Team:** Yuefeng Hao (PI); ORNL collaborators listed in hao-lab.md (Jiafu Mao, Xiaoying Shi, Yaoping Wang, Daniel M. Ricciuto, Peter E. Thornton, Forrest M. Hoffman; participation and funding mechanism to be confirmed); Yifan Gao and Shi Jin for the large-load use case.

**Research question and approach.** Do compound flash drought-heat events in the Tennessee Valley cut summer cooling-water availability on weeks-to-months timescales in ways that siting assumptions based on annual or HUC2 averages miss? There are four work packages: (1) E3SM-RRM/ELM compound-extreme runs over the Southeast; (2) ET, T/ET and WUE recovery constraints from AmeriFlux and BMA-merged ET products; (3) a drought-regime surrogate for large ensembles (B2); and (4) sub-basin, seasonal water availability and cooling-water stress as inputs to data center and SMR siting.

**Closest existing work and gap.** PNNL's BER-funded IM3/GCAM-USA work covers data center water at state or HUC2 scale, focused on the West ([OSTI 2998851](https://www.osti.gov/dataexplorer/biblio/dataset/2998851); [OSTI 2589826](https://www.osti.gov/dataexplorer/biblio/dataset/2589826)). Alston, Love and Haider model data center energy and water for Michigan ([arXiv 2609.25437](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.25437)). E3SMv2's North American RRM was built "to inform the US energy sector about changes in water availability... heat waves" ([Tang et al., GMD 2023](https://gmd.copernicus.org/articles/16/3953/2023/)), but no Southeastern compound flash drought-heat application was found. None found couples ESM drought projections to large-load siting.

**Novelty.** Real, provided the hypothesis is about Earth-system predictability and optimization is the use case.

**Why us.** The PI is a co-author on the submitted overview of the E3SMv3 regionally refined configuration (*JAMES*, under review). The PI is lead author of CIVE v1.0 (*Ecological Indicators*, second revision) and PI of the DOE/ORNL vulnerability grant ($229,835, 5 years). The PI is also PI of the 104b TDEC data center + SMR water grant and the ISSE footprint grant, and leads two students who are building Tennessee Valley siting models. No other team found holds all of these.

**Fundability.** It mirrors the budget request's "target regions," "water availability for energy," "multi-sector dynamics" and "AI surrogate components." Program policy factors include "PI not previously supported by SC"; whether a lab subcontract counts as SC support is unknown.

**Risks.** BER may see the project as applied energy work unless the science leads. Reviewers will ask why not IM3; the answer is a different region, ESM extremes and sub-annual timing. The EESM budget is small. Both students are new.

**Verdict: Pursue.** Send a one-page concept to a BER EESM program manager first, keep the narrative to 15 pages or fewer, and submit before 2027-04-01.

###### G1. Beyond soil-moisture recovery: thresholds, transpiration shifts and lagged carbon-water recovery after flash drought in humid Southeastern ecosystems — Pursue

**Team:** Yuefeng Hao (PI); ORNL E3SM collaborators (to be confirmed); a new hydrology graduate student to be budgeted. Gao and Jin work on siting and should not be counted as hydrology personnel. Shi Jin could contribute a scientifically justified ML sub-aim for detecting regime shifts.

**Research question and approach.** H1: humid forests cross from energy-limited to water-limited ET only briefly, and the threshold shifts under concurrent heat (high VPD). H2: T/ET rises under heat during onset and stays perturbed after soil moisture recovers. H3: GPP and ET recovery lag soil-moisture recovery, with the lag set by VPD and refill of deep storage. H4: E3SM's land model reproduces recovery timing only when VPD-stomatal and deep-water processes are represented. Methods: AmeriFlux flux towers plus multi-source remote sensing; an ensemble of Priestley–Taylor and complementary-relationship models merged by BMA to quantify structural ET uncertainty during extremes; benchmarking with ORNL.

**Closest existing work and gap.** Zhang et al. analyzed 151 FLUXNET flash-drought events and found that WUE rises during recovery in forests but not in croplands ([HESS 2020](https://hess.copernicus.org/articles/24/5579/2020/)). Flash droughts with extreme heat recover more slowly ([Nature Geoscience 2025](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41561-025-01719-y)). A soil-moisture threshold controls coupling during drought-heatwaves ([Commun. Earth Environ. 2025](https://www.nature.com/articles/s43247-025-02977-9)). Stoy's award partitions ET across the US but not specifically during compound extremes ([NSF 2422397](https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/showAward?AWD_ID=2422397)). No funded project tests whether recovery follows soil moisture in humid Southeastern forests against ESM process representation.

**Novelty.** It tests a paradigm, which matches the solicitation's "transformative" language. Without the recovery and humid-regime framing, it would overlap 2414601 and 2303458.

**Why us.** The PI's flash-drought WUE and recovery paper (*AFM* 2026) and AGU 2024 Missouri Ozark AmeriFlux talk; the heatwave hydrology paper (*J. Hydrol.* 2024); drought-recovery papers (*J. Hydrol.* 2023, China and Korea); the ET-model portfolio (soil-water-index Priestley–Taylor, *AFM* 2019; complementary relationship + BMA, *AFM* 2019; BMA drivers of ET, *J. Hydrol.* 2022; conductance-based ET partitioning, *J. Hydrol.* 2021); and ORNL E3SM collaborators. Few NSF-funded flash-drought groups pair observed recovery diagnostics with an ESM team.

**Fundability.** It is foundational critical-zone and land-atmosphere science, produces a public event-recovery dataset (a stated measure of success), and benefits from the early-career priority.

**Risks.** Southeastern flux-tower coverage of the 2016 and 2019 flash droughts was not checked. The PI's ISE affiliation may raise questions in EAR, which the hydrology publication record answers. PT, CR and BMA may look like legacy methods unless tied to hypotheses.

**Verdict: Pursue.** Email a one-page summary to WaLCZ@nsf.gov and ask about typical award size.

###### E1. Drought- and heat-robust co-design of data center cooling technology, water sourcing and operations with grid-attributed water — Pursue

**Team:** Yuefeng Hao (PI), Yifan Gao, Shi Jin; Mingzhou Jin as possible optimization collaborator (not confirmed); a thermal-engineering Co-PI is needed (none in the talent pool).

**Research question and approach.** For a fixed set of candidate Tennessee Valley sites, which mix of cooling technologies (evaporative, hybrid or adiabatic, dry, liquid) and water sources minimizes a new **drought-conditioned, stress-weighted total (direct + indirect) water** metric at acceptable cost and reliability? The model is a two-stage distributionally robust optimization. Stage 1 chooses cooling portfolio and water source; stage 2 chooses hourly wet/dry switching and load flexibility. Ambiguity sets come from compound flash-drought and heatwave scenarios. Indirect water is decision-dependent: the cooling choice changes grid load, and indirect water is attributed at generator level across the TVA/SERC fleet, including derating at river-temperature limits. Following the cross-call partition, regional siting and capacity expansion stay in CAREER K1. E3 (reclaimed water) is an aim here, and E2 (SMR) is a case-study module.

**Closest existing work and gap.** Vabson et al. site data centers by county with a deterministic base model ([arXiv 2601.16315](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.16315)). Xiao, You et al. analyze national scenarios, estimating 731–1,125 million m³/yr for AI servers ([Nature Sustainability](https://re.public.polimi.it/retrieve/536a055b-d8ab-4b86-bd4d-88facfaaf2ae/s41893-025-01681-y.pdf)). "Balancing Bits and Drops" uses static county-month AWARE stress factors to evaluate, not optimize ([arXiv 2607.22617](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22617)). Alston et al. found that air cooling halves total water but raises indirect water by a third in Michigan, but they assess rather than optimize ([arXiv 2609.25437](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.25437)). None treats cooling choice as a decision that moves water between the site and the grid under drought-heat uncertainty.

**Novelty.** Decision-dependent indirect water under hydro-climate ambiguity, plus a new metric. This is a methods contribution, not a relabeling.

**Why us.** The PI's flash-drought and heatwave science supplies the uncertainty model. The PI's submitted electricity-related water screening paper supplies the grid-water attribution base. Gao's robust siting and Jin's tariff-aware Tennessee Valley models supply the optimization base. The ISSE and 104b grants supply data access and a state-agency stakeholder.

**Fundability.** It matches "AI modeling... novel metrics," the early-career priority and "novel connections across scientific domains." A 3-year budget of about $400K fits the observed norm.

**Risks.** The program director may route it to CMMI (operations research) or to CBET Transport Phenomena (cooling hardware). Keep water-resource limits (withdrawal and consumption caps, basin depletion, thermal limits) at the core. Credible cooling performance curves need a thermal Co-PI. The PI's submitted paper may overlap Alston et al. and must be distinguished from it.

**Verdict: Pursue.** Send a one-page summary to cbet-ewre@nsf.gov stressing water-resource management, and run a targeted Scopus search ("distributionally robust" + "data center" + "water") before writing.

###### C1. Siting AI data centers under endogenous rules (AMDO) — Pursue after program-director email

**Team:** Yifan Gao, Shi Jin, Yuefeng Hao; Mingzhou Jin as the only listed optimization collaborator (Co-PI role not confirmed).

**Research question and approach.** How should a planner site and expand capacity when (i) the chance of a moratorium or tariff change in a jurisdiction rises with the MW already sited and water already withdrawn there, spreading spatially; (ii) interconnection-queue information is revealed only by entering the queue; and (iii) substation and basin water headroom tighten with the planner's own decisions? The model class is multistage stochastic or distributionally robust programs with decision-dependent feasible regions. Contributions are decomposition, cuts and bounds on the value of modeling endogeneity, with an empirical hazard model fitted to moratorium and opposition data. C3 is one thrust, and the Tennessee Valley is the testbed.

**Closest existing work and gap.** Data center siting under queue delays treats delay as an exogenous scenario ([Abdelhady et al., ESCAPE 2026](https://psecommunity.org/wp-content/plugins/wpor/includes/file/2606/LAPSE-2026.0251-1v1.pdf); [Shao et al., arXiv 2510.25118](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.25118); [Kim et al., Nat. Commun. 2026](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-026-72324-9)). Decision-dependent facility location makes demand endogenous, not the feasible set ([Başçiftçi et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1912.05577); [Pantuso 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.09816); [NSF 2534745](https://api.nsf.gov/services/v1/awards/2534745.json)). Stakeholder-approval constraints are static ([NSF 2620205](https://api.nsf.gov/services/v1/awards/2620205.json)). The motivation is strong: at least 75 projects worth about $130B were blocked or delayed in Q1 2026, and statewide moratorium bills appeared in 14 states ([Data Center Watch](https://datacenterwatch.org/q1-2026)).

**Novelty.** Genuinely methodological. No facility-location model with a spatially contagious, decision-dependent regulatory hazard was found (web search only).

**Why us.** Both student papers provide the base models: Gao's robust siting under queue uncertainty and Jin's tariff- and moratorium-aware Tennessee Valley siting. Gao's NLP background can build the event data. The ISSE grant measures the noise, water and land-market drivers of local acceptance.

**Fundability.** It fits AMDO's "analytical methods to aid decision-making" with AI. It is not manufacturing, so the program director must confirm fit.

**Risks.** The team has a thin OR-theory record. The PI's 15 papers are in hydrology, climate and energy reviews, and both students are new. The hazard is hard to identify from few events. Strong theory groups (Minnesota, Pantuso) are competitors. Mitigate with preliminary computational results from the two student papers.

**Verdict: Pursue after a program-director email.** Submit after at least one student paper is out.

###### K1. Siting AI computing infrastructure under hydro-climate extremes: robust planning of coupled compute-power-cooling-water systems (ENG/CMMI-EBE) — Pursue

**Team:** Yuefeng Hao (sole PI). Students Yifan Gao and Shi Jin. Collaborators by single-sentence letters only: ORNL (E3SM scenarios) and Mingzhou Jin (optimization mentoring); none confirmed.

**Research question and approach.** How should multi-decade siting and capacity plans for data centers and co-located power account for nonstationary, spatially correlated compound extremes (heat-drought, low flow) that shrink cooling water and tighten thermal-discharge limits across a shared basin and grid at the same time? There are three thrusts. (i) Generate extreme scenarios from observations, remote sensing and E3SM-class projections. (ii) Build correlated-hazard robust or distributionally robust siting and capacity models with withdrawal and thermal-discharge constraints, extending the Gao and Jin models. (iii) Model moving policy constraints as uncertainty. Thrust (iii) must stay light so it does not duplicate AMDO C1.

**Education.** A "siting under extremes" data-science studio in IE 465/565 Applied Data Science; AI-for-infrastructure cases in IE 591; statistics-of-extremes modules in IE 200. The policy activity is the TDEC decision outputs.

**Closest existing work and gap.** Data center CAREER awards are all operational ([NSF 2541996](https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/showAward?AWD_ID=2541996), [NSF 2544321](https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/showAward?AWD_ID=2544321), [NSF 2340042](https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/showAward?AWD_ID=2340042), [NSF 2045641](https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/showAward?AWD_ID=2045641)). Energy-water CAREER precedents predate AI data centers ([NSF 1845931](https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/showAward?AWD_ID=1845931), [NSF 1847404](https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/showAward?AWD_ID=1847404)). Existing siting tools are screening indices ([PESGM 2026](https://index.mirasmart.com/PESGM2026/PDFfiles/PESGM2026-001928.pdf)) or colocation economics ([NSF 2603293](https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/showAward?AWD_ID=2603293)). No NSF-funded project that treats hydro-climate extremes as the uncertainty in data center siting was found. That is a statement about NSF awards, not proof that no paper exists.

**Novelty.** Foundational methods for siting interdependent compute-power-water infrastructure under spatially correlated hydro-climate extremes.

**Why us.** The PI has published on flash drought, heatwaves, ET and terrestrial water storage, and is also PI of two data center water grants in one basin (104b TDEC, ISSE). The PI has an ORNL E3SM collaboration, supervises two students already writing Tennessee Valley siting papers, and teaches the three courses the education plan uses.

**Fundability.** It is an integrated research-education plan in an ENG program whose scope ("water, energy... extreme events, cascading effects") fits almost verbatim, and it supports a budget of $500K or more.

**Risks.** Eligibility is unconfirmed. The optimization record is mostly the students' unpublished papers, so get at least one siting paper submitted before July 2027. **Verdict: Pursue.** Confirm eligibility with the Department Head first, then email the EBE and EWRE program contacts to choose between K1 and K2.

##### Ideas: USDA NIFA AFRI A1712 Rapid Response to Weather Events

**Key call rules and the qualifying event.** A1712 funds only **Extension or Integrated** projects (Standard or FASE grants), **12 months, at most $300,000 including indirect costs**. An application "must be submitted within 45 calendar days after a weather event or disaster", must "directly address effects associated with a recent weather event", and must include a statement on timing and relevance when the event is prolonged. One or more deliverables must be implemented **within 90 days of award**, the narrative is limited to **7 pages**, adoption potential must be measurable, and the program "limits applications to **one per PD per funding cycle**". On the 2026-10-20 map D2+ is 48.15%, D3+ 18.80%, and the first **D4 (1.16%)** appeared ([USDM TN statistics](https://usdmdataservices.unl.edu/api/StateStatistics/GetDroughtSeverityStatisticsByAreaPercent?aoi=47&startdate=8/1/2026&enddate=10/25/2026&statisticsType=1)).
